kaigo-atomic-oral-details.heading: Oral care and dentures: keep the whole mouth clean
paragraphs: Oral care cleans teeth and the mouth to help prevent cavities, gum disease and bad breath. It also reduces oral bacteria, supports saliva and taste, and helps appetite and eating. However, oral care alone does not completely prevent aspiration pneumonia or remove the need for swallowing assessment.

Before starting, explain the care and check oral condition and the support method. Observe gums, mucosa, remaining teeth and food residue while cleaning gently in small sections without missing areas. With hemiplegia, pay attention to food remaining on the paralyzed side. Report observed locations of bleeding, swelling or pain and the person’s complaints to healthcare professionals.

The material’s rinsing stage does not mean asking everyone to rinse unchanged. Individually check whether the person can rinse, spit out and maintain posture, selecting methods through oral and swallowing assessment and the plan. If difficult, do not force water into the mouth; check with the person responsible.

Stabilize posture and head position, considering aspiration risk and avoiding forced chin elevation. Examples of facing at eye level or supporting the head from behind illustrate support position and stability. Aspiration here means swallowed material entering the airway below the vocal cords; it differs from dysphagia, which means impaired swallowing function. A standing position alone does not prevent aspiration. Match care to individual condition and a trained method.
A pencil-like toothbrush grip is an example for controlling force. Rather than rubbing hard, ask about sensation and match movement to teeth and gums. Grip alone does not determine safety.

Sponge brushes and similar tools are selected according to oral condition and professional guidance. Do not assume they always clean as effectively as toothbrushes. Check instructions, suitability and condition before and after use. Watch for problems such as a loose sponge; do not use abnormal equipment and tell the person responsible. Knowing a tool’s name differs from safe use.

This section concerns removable dentures replacing missing teeth. Complete dentures replace all teeth and partial dentures some teeth, with upper and lower versions. Food and dirt also collect on dentures. Rinsing only the removed appliance does not complete all oral care.

Remove and clean dentures after meals or at times specified in the person’s plan. The material shows brushing off dirt and rinsing under running water. In practice, use brushes, water and any cleaners suitable for the denture material, following product and dental-professional instructions. After removal, clean remaining teeth and oral mucosa with suitable methods too. Check the dentures and inside of the mouth separately.

The material gives storage examples involving clean containers, water and cleaners. Consider cracking from drying while checking material, dental instructions and cleaner conditions. Do not independently dry dentures, disinfect with boiling water or soak in unsuitable liquids. Report pain or wounds; care workers must not grind dentures to repair them.

[Learning check] If the person says, “I washed my dentures, but not my remaining teeth yet,” distinguish completed and remaining parts. Respect independent actions and discuss necessary help. Actual care follows individual assessment, plan and facility instruction.

kaigo-atomic-bath-sequence.heading: Connect checks during and after bathing
paragraphs: During bathing, keep checking condition, expression, skin and feelings. Alongside neck, armpits, groin and feet, examine actual skin folds and areas prone to retained dirt. An unmarked area in a diagram does not mean it need not be washed.

Use accompaniment and equipment suited to condition to prevent falls. Cover needed areas with towels or similar items to respect modesty. The hemiplegia example places the worker on the paralyzed side, but actual position and assistance depend on ability, equipment and plan.

Before pouring water, check temperature using appropriate methods and equipment, and ask about heat and discomfort. One staff hand check does not establish continued safety for the person. If they say it is hot, stop pouring and recheck temperature and condition. With altered sensation, do not rely on complaints alone; follow the individual safe checking method.

The material shows gradually pouring from extremities toward the center and starting on the nonparalyzed side with hemiplegia. This differs from deciding where the worker stands to support movement. Do not apply memorized steps to everyone; check responses, facilities and individual methods as you proceed.

When washing, lather cleanser appropriately and avoid strong rubbing. Check dirt and skin folds and rinse cleanser away fully. Let the person perform possible parts, and review methods if pain or discomfort occurs.

The bathtub-entry example starts from the nonparalyzed side with hemiplegia. After entry, check stable posture and support the paralyzed side, which may float, as needed. Entry does not complete assistance. Do not leave someone who needs support alone, and continue observing condition through expressions and other clues.

Suddenly standing from a bathtub can cause unsteadiness associated with orthostatic hypotension. Assist slow position changes in a suitable way and observe afterward too. With abnormalities, stop bathing and request help or healthcare contact according to facility procedures. Check heat for the final rinse too.

For hair washing, wet the hair, use suitably lathered shampoo and wash gently with finger pads, not nails against the scalp. Keep water and shampoo out of eyes, rinse residue and ask about discomfort.

After bathing, gently press with a dry towel rather than rubbing, carefully drying skin folds too. Arrange clothing to avoid chilling. Moisturize dry-prone skin according to the plan. Moisturizing differs from leaving water in folds. Report wounds or abnormalities rather than independently applying a new product and considering the matter settled.

Use a hair dryer according to product instructions, checking temperature, distance and airflow location. A diagram using the worker’s hand as a guide does not guarantee burn prevention. After drying, check condition and comfort and follow the individual rest and fluid plan. Distinguish finished washing from completed post-bath checks.

kaigo-atomic-partial-perineal-wash.heading: Partial and intimate washing: cleanliness and privacy
paragraphs: A hand bath washes hands and a foot bath washes feet. Prepare a stable posture with a reachable basin or a container into which the feet fit comfortably. Use seated or bed-based methods suited to condition and let the person perform possible parts.

Prepare suitably warm water and clean supplies. After washing, rinse off cleanser and gently remove moisture. Do not reuse water or equipment from another person or dirty area unchanged for clean care. The names hand or foot bath identify scope, not exemption from hygiene checks.

The material notes that nails soften after partial baths and may be easier to cut. Softness alone does not authorize cutting. Check nails, surrounding skin, illnesses and instructions; consult healthcare professionals about abnormalities.

Intimate areas collect excreta and sweat. Continued soiling may cause odor or bacterial infection, so cleanliness matters. Do not diagnose infection from odor alone. Explain purpose and method, obtain consent and cover unnecessary areas for privacy. These areas are temperature-sensitive; the material gives water close to body temperature as an example. Staff sensation or room temperature alone cannot determine suitability. Follow individual condition and the specified checking method.

The female-care example washes from the urethral area toward the anus. Do not move back and forth with the same surface; change surfaces or materials to avoid carrying anal contamination toward the urethra. Beyond remembering “front to back,” check what a clean surface touches.

In male care, check dirt and skin condition around the scrotum and skin folds too. Maintain cleanliness through consent, the individual plan and trained methods. Report pain or skin abnormalities to healthcare professionals. Do not forcefully pull skin or tissues.

After washing, gently press dry and observe redness, pain or wounds. Report abnormal locations and complaints to healthcare professionals. Disposable gloves do not permit touching a clean site with a contaminated surface. When moving from dirty to clean work, appropriately remove gloves, perform hand hygiene and change to necessary fresh gloves or materials.

[Learning check] Wearing gloves while returning from the anus toward the urethra with the same wiping surface does not establish cleanliness. Check direction separately from the clean state of surfaces and supplies. Actual care follows individual assessment and plan and facility procedures and training.

kaigo-atomic-icf.heading: Use ICF to consider functioning together with environment
paragraphs: The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) organizes functioning, disability and health to understand the person’s whole life. It does not determine abilities from a diagnosis alone. Consider health condition together with body functions and structures, activities and participation.

Body functions are physical and mental functions. Body structures are parts such as limbs and organs. Activity means performing tasks or actions such as dressing or housework. Participation means involvement in life situations such as community gatherings or work. Do not replace these with identical meanings.

Environmental factors include housing, helpers, community resources and services, and attitudes. An environment may facilitate or hinder activity. Personal factors include age, experience, personality and values. People with the same diagnosis or age do not necessarily need identical support.

Two-way arrows show interaction between components. Bodily functions affect activity, while environment and participation opportunities also affect what can actually be done. Avoid the one-direction assumption that illness uniformly rules out activity and participation.

[Learning example] The person wants a reading group, but a door is difficult to open when entering in a wheelchair. Record mobility, the door as an environmental barrier and the wish to participate separately. Ask wishes and check accessible routes and needed support with relevant people. Do not treat the barrier only as a bodily problem.

The material illustrates suitably sloped routes helping mobility-equipment users access transport. A ramp’s presence alone does not establish safe use. Check actual slope, route, equipment, abilities and wishes when selecting support.

The personal-factor illustration includes sex and age, but these alone do not determine preferences or independence. Handle necessary information with clear purpose and sharing scope and appropriate conditions such as consent. Actual support follows assessment and the individual plan.

kaigo-atomic-motor-disability.heading: Physical disability: check movement and comprehension separately
paragraphs: Physical disability involves impaired limb or trunk movement from illness, accident or other causes, creating daily-life or social difficulties. Causes include brain or spinal-cord injury, limb injury, bone, joint or spinal deformity and joint contracture. Contracture means restricted joint movement. The name alone does not determine a mobility-assistance method.

Affected regions and severity differ individually. Difficulty moving fingers differs from understanding speech. Cognitive or intellectual impairment may coexist, but movement difficulty alone does not justify treating someone as unable to understand. Check each ability and desired support.

Canes, wheelchairs and prosthetic limbs serve different purposes. A prosthesis replaces part of a missing limb. Select equipment suited to health, abilities, life goals and environment, with necessary adjustment and use training. Possession alone does not establish safe use.

[Learning example] The person has difficulty moving a hand but answers questions clearly. Speak directly to them first and provide an accessible response method and time. If family help is needed, ask which parts the person wants help with. Do not exclude them from conversation because of hand movement.

Share body location, cause and current abilities separately to inform support. Actual assistance follows assessment, the individual plan and facility instruction. This explanation does not guarantee mastery of transfers or equipment handling.

kaigo-atomic-hearing-disability.heading: Hearing disability: choose an accessible method together
paragraphs: Hearing disability means absent or reduced hearing creating difficulties in life or participation. The affected point along the ear-to-brain pathway, severity and onset vary. Age or hearing-aid use alone does not show which sounds are heard or how much language is understood.

Hearing aids collect and amplify sounds to support hearing. They do not completely restore prior hearing or separate all useful sounds from background noise. Do not assume an explanation was understood because one is worn; ask about hearing and effective communication. Confirm adjustments and use with the responsible professional.

Speak from the front in as quiet a setting as possible with expressions and mouth visible. Consider a known better-hearing ear too. Speak slowly and clearly without excessive volume. Do not rely only on louder speech; check background noise and responses.

Written conversation uses writing; sign language conveys meaning through hands, fingers, facial expressions and other features; lipreading uses mouth movement and related clues. Combine text, signing, lipreading and hearing aids in useful ways. Not everyone can use each method equally.

Choose methods by checking readable writing, language, vision, signing or lipreading experience and wishes. Do not assume everyone with reduced hearing signs or understands everything from a visible mouth. After communication, check what was received with minimal burden.

[Learning example] Instructions are not understood in a noisy room despite a hearing aid. First ask what makes communication difficult and discuss quieter surroundings or another method. Check whether text helps too. Support follows individual assessment and plan; staff must not independently alter device settings.

kaigo-atomic-aphasia.heading: Aphasia: distinguish listening, speaking, reading and writing
paragraphs: Language and speech disorders broadly concern difficult verbal communication from brain-language functions or speech-organ problems. Aphasia is difficulty with previously acquired language after damage to brain-language regions or similar causes, sometimes after stroke. Listening comprehension, speaking, reading comprehension and writing may be affected differently. Check difficulties individually.

Few spoken words alone do not establish absent comprehension, unwillingness to talk or total cognitive loss. Aphasia also differs from difficulty moving speech muscles alone. Language and speech-production problems can overlap, requiring appropriate professional assessment.

Speak one point at a time in short, clear language and wait for a response. Do not interrupt intended communication by correcting every small word error. Yes/no questions or choices can help when suited to the person, but do not interpret answers for staff convenience.

Try pictures, photographs, gestures, choice boards, writing or support devices according to retained abilities and wishes. Reading and writing may also be difficult in aphasia; inability to speak does not guarantee ability to write. Share usable methods with professionals and the team.

[Learning example] After a stroke, verbal responses are few, but when shown pictures of two activities the person selects the same picture. Record sparse speech separately from observed picture choice. Check whether that choice expresses a wish using an accessible method. One selection does not evaluate all language function.

Allow time to confirm wishes rather than inventing them because staff cannot wait for words. Seek ways to participate and tell the person responsible observed responses and unknowns. Actual support follows assessment, the individual plan and professional guidance.

134.title: Oral care and dentures: keep the whole mouth clean
objectives: Clean the mouth and removable dentures with methods suited to each.
Explain posture, equipment and storage conditions and reportable changes.
134.context: Study teeth, mucosa and dentures separately. Do not use posture or equipment examples as universal procedures.
134.artCaption: The person and worker consult written materials. The picture does not show oral inspection or denture cleaning itself.

135.title: Connect checks during and after bathing
objectives: Connect checks of condition, water and posture during bathing with checks afterward.
Distinguish worker position from the side on which water application starts.
135.context: Learn checks from bathing through hair washing, drying and rest. Adapt procedures to responses and individual support methods.
135.artCaption: A worker prepares water, towels and other supplies beside a bed. This does not show completed bathtub assistance or water-temperature checks.

136.title: Partial and intimate washing: cleanliness and privacy
objectives: Explain partial-wash scope and clean–dirty boundaries in intimate washing.
Distinguish unconfirmed specific handling from observations and consultation needs.
136.context: This unit covers partial baths and intimate cleanliness. Some specific male-washing descriptions remain unconfirmed; do not infer and perform them from pictures.
136.artCaption: Staff stand beside clean supplies and a used-item container. The image alone guarantees neither supply cleanliness nor washing technique.

137.title: Use ICF to consider functioning together with environment
objectives: Distinguish body functions and structures, activity, participation and environmental factors.
Consider support through goals together with environmental barriers.
137.context: Organize relationships between the person and environment rather than judging life from diagnosis. Use the project’s reading-group example to distinguish activity and participation.
137.artCaption: The person and worker inspect a route near an entrance step, considering movement and surroundings together.

138.title: Physical disability: check movement and comprehension separately
objectives: Separate movement difficulties from checks of comprehension and wishes.
Explain equipment selection, adjustment and use-training needs.
138.context: Study causes and individual variation and the importance of directly asking for the person’s responses and wishes.
138.artCaption: Staff explain with a body model. The image does not determine personal abilities or transfer-equipment suitability.

139.title: Hearing disability: choose an accessible method together
objectives: Ask about helpful communication and arrange an accessible sound environment.
Distinguish wearing a hearing aid from understanding an explanation.
139.context: Hearing and accessible methods vary. Choose communication with the person instead of relying on volume alone.
139.artCaption: The person speaks while a worker listens and takes notes. The image does not establish hearing-aid use or degree of hearing.

140.title: Aphasia: distinguish listening, speaking, reading and writing
objectives: Separate four language aspects and specifically record observed responses.
Select suitable pictures, gestures or text and check wishes.
140.context: Learn aphasia-related difficulties and support using retained abilities. Picture choice alone does not evaluate all language.
140.artCaption: Staff show drink or food pictures and wait. Presenting images alone does not confirm wishes.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-oral-details.prompt: Which approach to oral care is appropriate?
options: Clean removed dentures mean all oral checks are complete.
Remaining teeth need no cleaning for a denture user.
The denture-washing method suits all mucosa unchanged.
Check remaining teeth and mucosa too and provide care suited to each.
rationales: Denture cleaning and inside-mouth checks differ; unchecked areas remain.
Remaining teeth need cleaning; partial dentures do not remove that need.
Dentures and mucosa differ; identical tools or methods are not always suitable.
Distinguish completed and unchecked areas to consider whole-mouth care.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-oral-details.reading: [Learning example] Partial dentures were removed and washed. The remaining teeth and oral mucosa have not been checked.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bath-sequence.prompt: What is the appropriate next response?
options: A staff hand check means personal responses need not inform temperature checks.
Stop pouring and recheck condition and temperature.
The initial check proves safety until bathing ends.
After the complaint, checking hemiplegia alone is sufficient.
rationales: Staff sensation alone cannot establish suitability for the person.
Acknowledge the complaint and check before continuing.
Temperature and condition require ongoing checks; one check does not guarantee the whole course.
Hemiplegia is one fact, not a substitute for addressing heat or checking water.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bath-sequence.reading: [Learning example] A worker checked water by hand. When it was poured, the person said, “It is too hot.”

options: Gloves alone do not maintain cleanliness; check direction and clean surfaces and materials.
Gloves make using the same surface in either direction clean.
Knowing a back-and-forth direction removes checks of surface contamination.
Hand hygiene may be omitted after removing gloves.
rationales: Clean surfaces and a direction avoiding return of contamination are needed. Gloves do not replace hygiene or dirty–clean boundaries.
Contaminated surfaces can transfer dirt even with gloves.
Check both direction and surface to avoid bringing contamination toward the urethra.
Hand hygiene remains necessary after glove removal.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-partial-perinea.reading: [Learning example] During intimate washing, a gloved worker intends to return toward the urethra with the surface used on the anal area.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-icf.prompt: Which description uses the ICF perspective?
options: Determine inability to participate from diagnosis alone.
Omit the door because it is outside the body.
Separate mobility, participation wishes and the door barrier and check needed support.
Fixing the environment always removes checks of wishes or movement.
rationales: Diagnosis alone cannot explain activity, participation and environment relationships.
Environmental factors affect activity and participation; the difficult door matters.
This distinguishes interacting personal and environmental aspects.
Environmental changes and checks of wishes and abilities must be considered together.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-icf.reading: [Learning example] The person wants to join a reading group and approaches using a wheelchair, but the door is difficult to open.

options: Hand difficulty limits asking wishes to the family.
Speak directly to the person and check an accessible response method and desired support.
A clear reply proves independence in every movement.
Equipment removes individual movement or comprehension checks.
rationales: Movement difficulty alone does not establish inability to understand or express wishes.
This separates movement from comprehension and preserves participation.
Clear answers do not prove all movements can be performed without help.
Equipment presence alone establishes neither safety nor individual ability.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-motor-disabilit.reading: [Learning example] The person has difficulty moving a hand but answers clearly. Staff intend to ask only family about wishes without asking the person.

options: Record understanding because a hearing aid is worn.
A hearing aid removes checks of room noise.
Always switch only to lipreading without asking experience.
Ask about difficulties and wishes and discuss a quieter place or another accessible method.
rationales: Wearing an aid differs from understanding instructions.
Noise affects hearing and may not be fully removed by hearing aids.
Lipreading accessibility varies; ask about experience and wishes.
Check environment and useful methods together. Select text only after checking usability.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-hearing-disabil.reading: [Learning example] Instructions have not reached a hearing-aid user in a noisy room. Staff are considering only raising their voices.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-aphasia.prompt: How should this observation be handled?
options: Few words make picture responses entirely unusable for checking wishes.
Repeated picture choice completes listening, speaking, reading and writing assessment.
Record verbal and picture responses separately and check wishes through a suitable method.
Speech difficulty guarantees written answers are possible.
rationales: Seek retained abilities rather than dismissing picture responses because words are few.
One selection does not assess every language aspect.
Accurately record observed scope and support participation and wish checking.
Aphasia may affect reading and writing too; written communication needs individual suitability checks.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-aphasia.reading: [Learning example] After a stroke, verbal replies are few, but with two activity pictures the person selects the same one.
